title: Theosis (CCC 460)
hookLine: the Son of God became man so that we might share his divinity

lines: TO FORGIVE, TO SHOW THE WAY.
cards: Ask a room of churchgoers why God became man, and the answers come quickly. To forgive our sins. To show us the way.

To die for us. All of those are in the Catechism. But in one short paragraph, number four hundred sixty, it gives a reason that's easy to read past: the Word became flesh to make us partakers of the divine nature.
Not just forgiven. Brought into God's own life. The Eastern churches we've been visiting have a word for this, and they treasure it.

teach.b: Underneath the paragraph is a line from scripture.

The Second Letter of Peter says, in the Douay-Rheims, that God has given us most great and precious promises, "that by these you may be made partakers of the divine nature." A partaker is someone who has a share.
The Catechism calls saints as witnesses: Saint Irenaeus, Saint Athanasius and Saint Thomas Aquinas, West and East side by side, all saying the same startling thing.
Athanasius's line, in an old English translation, is short enough to memorize: "For He was made man that we might be made God." That line can be heard wrong.
It doesn't mean people become a second God, or stop being creatures, or dissolve into God like sugar in tea.

teach.h: IRON IN THE FIRE: GLOWING, STILL IRON.
teach.b: Eastern writers explain it with a picture: iron left in a fire. It glows, it burns, it gives off heat and light, and it's still iron. The fire is the fire's own; the iron shares it.
That's theosis: being drawn into God's life by grace, while remaining yourself, a creature, a person. It sheds light on what we've seen these past days.

teach.h: HE WAS MADE MAN THAT WE MIGHT BE MADE GOD.
teach.b: The icons show saints already shining with that light. The liturgy is heaven touching earth. Babies receive communion, and God's life is offered from the start.
Catholics in the West tend to say grace, sanctification, or sharing in the divine life. Catholics in the East say theosis. The Catechism puts both vocabularies on one page.

how: Eastern Catholics, like the Orthodox, speak of theosis as the goal of the Christian life; Latin Catholics usually speak of grace and sharing in the divine life, and the Catechism (CCC 460) presents both together.

games.q: a friend hears "he was made man that we might be made God" and asks if Christians think they'll become gods. what does the tradition say?
o: yes, each person becomes a separate god.
no: by grace we share God's life and remain creatures.
it's only poetry and means nothing.
games.why: Eastern and Western Christians alike read it as sharing in God's life by grace. the iron glows with the fire, and stays iron.

practice: Let the line come back slowly: he was made man that we might be made God. Don't analyze it; notice which word catches, man, made, God, we, and stay with that one word for a few breaths, like iron in the fire, still iron, glowing.
If you pray, simply rest in the line, words the Church has kept; if you don't, let it be a sentence someone believed enough to stake a life on, and keep it company.

wordCard.voice: Theosis. The Eastern Christian word for being drawn into God's own life by grace, made partakers of the divine nature while remaining creatures. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: deification, being drawn into God's life; the Eastern Christian word for what CCC 460 describes.

carryVoice: Your line: made sharers. A partaker isn't an owner, but someone given a share. Until tomorrow.
